new_statements.quote: With regard to the phonetic notation, stress is penultimate unless otherwise marked. [p. 141] ... Some dialects of Geser display additional innovations. In Pulau Panjang, for example, [f], the reflex of *p, has moved to [h]; *k shifted to [ʔ] whereas it is retained in Geser. In Kiandarat word-final *u shifted to [i] and was metathesised, yielding forms like [wait-a] stone < *batu, [suis-a] < *susu breast, etc. [fn 33, p. 138]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (24 pp., native text layer) opened; p. 141 = PDF p. 19 rendered and read as an image. The sentence is there exactly: 'With regard to the phonetic notation, stress is penultimate unless otherwise marked.' (the extracted text layer has lowercase 'with'; the page has capital W, so the reader's quote matches the page). Fn 33 on p. 138 (PDF p. 16) verified verbatim on the page image: 'Some dialects of Geser display additional innovations. In Pulau Panjang, for example, [f], the reflex of *p, has moved to [h]; *k shifted to [ʔ] whereas it is retained in Geser. In Kiandarat word-final *u shifted to [i] and was metathesised, yielding forms like [wait-a] stone < *batu, [suis-a] < *susu breast,…
new_statements.relation_note: Bati is not in the catalog and has no existing stress statements, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict. The work adds the first (weak) datum: a penultimate-by-default notation convention that covers the Geser language of which Bati/Kiandarat is treated as a dialect, with the Geser data taken from Selor. It does not describe Bati stress itself; a Bati-specific statement would have to come from Goward & Ellen 1981 (unpublished MS) or from the accents in Wallace's 1869 'Gah' list, neither of which this paper analyses. Best classed as a regional default, not a Bati record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A one-sentence transcription convention for the 200-item comparative wordlist of six East Seram languages (Seti, Bobot, Masiwang, Geser, Watubela, Banda): stress is on the penultimate syllable, and only deviations are marked with an acute. The Geser data come from the Selor variant, not from Bati/Kiandarat. Bati is never named in the paper; the only Bati-specific material is fn 33 on the Kiandarat dialect (a segmental metathesis fact, no stress) and an uncited reference to Goward & Ellen 1981, 'A wordlist of the Bati language' (MS). So the penultimate default is a regional default for the wordlist, not a Bati-specific description.
new_statements.exceptions: Acute marks in the appendix flag non-penultimate (final) stress in some Seti, Masiwang and Banda forms (e.g. Seti lúli-a 'bone', láha 'blood', tatán 'weep'; Masiwang ahás 'swim', mumáh 'yawn'; Banda erén 'come', omá 'come', moŋón 'dirty'); the Geser column on p. 142 carries no marks. Fn 28 p. 138 explains final stress in Banda metmetén 'black' as the trace of a fossilised genitive suffix -ni ~ -; No exceptions are given for Geser or for Bati/Kiandarat.
new_statements.identity_note: Collins 1986 never uses the name Bati. It treats the variety as the 'Kiandarat' dialect of Geser (fn 33, p. 138), which Loski & Loski 1989 (fn 31, p. 127) explicitly identify as 'the Kian Darat (our Bati)' dialect of Geser-Gorom; the defining feature Collins gives for Kiandarat (final *u > i with metathesis, waita 'stone', suisa 'breast') is the same correspondence Loski & Loski use to define Bati. The Geser column of Collins's wordlist, to which the penultimate-stress convention applies, is from Selor, not from Kiandarat/Bati. Collins's references also list Goward, N. & R. Ellen 1981, 'A wordlist of the Bati language', MS in the possession of the author (p. 139), not cited in the body.

sources.note: No Bati-specific statement; Bati data come only from Wallace 1869 and Ellen 1993 (Appendix A.8, p. 742). Regional generalisations only: p. 115 'While penultimate stress is the normal rule for Wallacean languages, words with penultimate schwa can have stress on other syllables'; p. 444 (Seram-Tanimbar-Bomberai chapter) 'Stress and/or tone is probably contrastive in some of the Bomberai languages, though the most common pattern in our data is penultimate stress/high tone.' Reproduces Wallace's accented Bati forms (bóia, lúme, wúan, kaúfei, mofánas, fúdia, faasí).

sources.note: Wordlist only. General convention on p. 471: 'Long, short, and accented syllables are marked in the usual way.'
